articles.title: Indonesian Cinema’s Next Chapter Is Reaching the World ‘Without Losing Our Cultural Identity,’ Says JAFF Market Director Linda Gozali
articles.summary: Indonesia’s film industry has momentum at home. JAFF Market director Linda Gozali wants to help it travel. Gozali runs the industry market attached to the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (JAFF), now in its third edition.
body: “Our next chapter is learning how to reach international audiences without losing our cultural identity,” Gozali tells Variety. “We aspire to become nationally indispensable, regionally relevant and internationally connected.”

Local hits have yet to translate into comparable business abroad, which Gozali puts down to producers and filmmakers treating the home market as their first priority. “Indonesia has learned how to win its own audiences,” she says, adding that plenty of untapped local viewers still need to be brought in.

Even so, Gozali says, a good share of Indonesian horror has sold across multiple territories, and independent films have been well received on the international festival circuit. She also notes that Indonesia is not alone in looking inward first, pointing to other populous countries such as China, India and Japan.
“Any growth should not be mistaken for maturity,” she says. “JAFF Market’s responsibility is to transform that growth into sustainability.”

articles.title: Southeast Asian Cinema’s Global Rise Needs Long-Term Backing to Last, Says JAFF Chief Ifa Isfansyah
articles.summary: The quality and international profile of Southeast Asian cinema have grown sharply, and Ifa Isfansyah, festival director of Indonesia’s Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (JAFF), wants countries to build on that by treating film as part of their cultural strategy.
body: He singles out the Philippines for its consistency in developing talent and keeping a presence abroad.

Isfansyah is also one of Indonesia’s leading independent producers. He founded Forka Films, formerly Fourcolours Films, in 2001, and his producing credits include Kamila Andini’s “Yuni” and “Before, Now & Then,” as well as her latest, “Four Seasons in Java,” which played Toronto’s Centerpiece program and Busan this year.

“I believe countries need to recognize cinema as an important part of their cultural strategy, not merely as an industry or a source of national prestige,” he says. “This requires long-term investment, institutional support, and a commitment to building sustainable connections with the international film community.”

JAFF’s 21st edition drew more than 1,000 submissions, from which the festival picked 254 films from 34 countries. The program runs under the theme “Influx,” opening with Lawrence Fajardo’s Filipino drama “Silenced Nights” and closing with Ueda Makoto’s Japanese comedy-drama “You Are the Film.”

articles.title: France Knights ‘Autobiography,’ ‘Tiger Stripes’ Producer Yulia Evina Bhara at JAFF Market
articles.summary: Indonesian producer Yulia Evina Bhara, whose credits include Venice title “Autobiography” and Cannes Critics’ Week winner “Tiger Stripes,” was named a Chevalier dans l’Ordre des Arts et des Lettres at a ceremony at JAFF Market in Yogyakarta.
body: France created the order in 1957, and its cinema honorees range from Agnès Varda, François Truffaut, Martin Scorsese and Isabelle Huppert to Indonesia’s Garin Nugroho. Filmmaker Joko Anwar received it last year.

“When I read the names of the people who received this before me, I felt very small,” Bhara said. “They are writers, painters, musicians, directors, and many of them are my heroes. So when the letter came, my first thought was, maybe this is a mistake. My second was, this is not only for me, and this is true. A film producer never works alone. A producer is like a person who builds a boat, but the boat only moves when people row together.”

In his address, Penone traced Bhara’s path from Way Kanan in Sumatra’s Lampung province through seven years of producing historical theater, a craft she taught herself, before she turned to film in 2012 with a foundation that used art to revisit the past. She set up KawanKawan Media in Jakarta in 2016, with international co-production at the core of the business from day one. The company’s name is Indonesian for “friends.”

articles.title: WWE Star Bronson Reed Dies at 38
articles.summary: WWE star Bronson Reed died Friday at the age of 38, the WWE confirmed in a statement. The Australian-born wrestler, whose real name was Jermaine Haley, died “due to medical complications,” the league said.
body: Haley was raised in Adelaide and got his start working “throughout Australia’s independent scene and wrestled for a number of local promotions, including International Wrestling Australia and Melbourne City Wrestling,” according to a report by Variety Australia.

Haley joined WWE in 2019 and made his first appearance on the league’s up-and-comers series “NXT.” He was released by WWE in 2021 but came back the following year and had remained active with the league until Friday.

Per Variety Australia, Haley “made his way into the main event scene in 2025 as part of The Vision faction, alongside Seth Rollins, fellow prospect Bron Breakker and arguably WWE’s greatest ever talker, Paul Heyman.”

In an interview with Rolling Stone AU/ZN last year, Haley said: “I think for me, a big change is when I got released from WWE and I came back, I sort of came back with a little bit of a chip on my shoulder, knowing that I need to be as confident as possible and show them I can do this. I’m supposed to be here,” according to Variety Australia.

articles.title: The little Welsh town that transformed a Strictly star's career
articles.summary: Layton Williams credits living and working in a small Welsh town with transforming his career.
body: The Bad Education actor spent months in Mold, Flintshire, rehearsing for the role of Angel in the musical Rent, which he said marked a turning point in his career.
"I've got to be honest, before I lived in Mold, I had not a clue that Mold was a place that existed, but I completely fell in love with it," he said.
Williams, from Bury in Greater Manchester, feels so connected to the town that he insisted on having a show at the Theatr Clwyd on his upcoming tour, Layton Live.
"The producers were like, 'we've never had a specific request to go to Mold, but we will make it happen'. And I said 'Thank you'," Williams said in an interview with Lucy Owen on BBC Radio Wales.

articles.title: Avengers: Doomsday has brought with it more ‘Marvel homework’ than ever. That’s just as it should be
articles.summary: Working out where returning hero Steve Rogers has been is only one of the multiversal puzzles fans must now get their heads around – which is catnip for the connoisseurs.
body: The cinema release of Avengers: Doomsday is now roughly three weeks away and, judging by the final trailer, we’re living in the one timeline where every loose end Marvel has left dangling for years is now worth tugging on. Even the ones we thought the studio had tied up rather nicely. Ever since it became apparent that Chris Evans’ Steve Rogers would be returning in the new film, along with next year’s sequel Avengers: Secret Wars, fans have been asking themselves: where exactly has he been all this time? Now, thanks to the latest footage, we’re beginning to get an idea, and we might also be starting to pick up clues as to why Doctor Doom would take an interest in his new postcode.

One of the most startling aspects of the new trailer is the arrival of the Fantastic Four, led by Pedro Pascal’s Reed Richards, on Rogers’ front lawn. We’ve known since the finale of Avengers: Endgame that Steve used Tony Stark’s newly discovered time-travelling tech to go back to the 1940s and live out his life with Peggy Carter during the events of that film – but until recently it seemed most likely that happened in good old Earth-616, the main Marvel Cinematic Universe continuity.

articles.title: Strong ‘I Play Rocky,’ ‘How to Rob a Bank’ KO and More: Amazon MGM Distribution Head on 2026 Highs and Lows
articles.summary: Kevin Wilson tells The Hollywood Reporter about the 'Rocky' origin story's "great start," 'How to Rob a Bank' underperforming ("Still trying to figure it out") and the 'Ali G' strategy: "That theatrical hurdle is just tough."
body: Amazon MGM Studios ‘ team is relishing the thrill of the theatrical fight as I Play Rocky looks to capitalize on its muscular start.

I Play Rocky is the latest release in a buzzy year for the studio, following the mammoth success of this spring’s Project Hail Mary — set for rerelease Dec. 11 as awards season comes out swinging — and a winning path for Verity. Amazon MGM also sparked recent conversation with its unusual release plan for Sacha Baron Cohen’s Ali G: Who Iz I?, which received a two-day theatrical run just before hitting Prime Video, and for its tough turnout for David Leitch’s How to Rob a Bank, the $40 million-budgeted heist film that opened earlier this month with just $5.1 million domestically.

During a conversation with The Hollywood Reporter conducted ahead of Thanksgiving, Amazon MGM head of domestic theatrical distribution Kevin Wilson shares insight into I Play Rocky’ s broad appeal and the hopes that it continues to find younger audiences after that impressive A+ CinemaScore. Wilson also weighs in on the releases for How to Rob a Bank, Ali G and David O. Russell’s Madden, not to mention the company’s big James Bond casting news.

articles.title: Alun Wyn Jones urges men to talk about hair loss after transplant
articles.summary: The former Wales captain said he wanted to encourage more men to talk openly about hair loss.
body: Rugby legend Alun Wyn Jones has urged men to open up about hair loss, saying he was "very comfortable" talking about the fact he has had a hair transplant.
Speaking one year since his operation, the former Wales and British and Irish Lions captain said men typically do not talk about the issue, but said "a lot of people" had spoken to him about it.
"I think it's important that people know there's a lot of people out there they can talk to," he said.
Jones played 158 times for Wales and 12 for the Lions, making him the most capped rugby player in history before he retired in 2023.

articles.title: Cozy escapism or festive trash? How Netflix holiday movies took over Christmas
articles.summary: The so-bad-it’s-good holiday film has become a new festive tradition. Stars Maddie Ziegler and Dennis Quaid explain why they’re so hard to resist. “With the state of the world right now, people want an escape,” says Maddie Ziegler.
body: In the film, Ziegler plays Maelyn – a restless twentysomething who finds herself trapped in a holiday time-loop, where she’s forced to relive the same Christmas at her family’s picturesque cabin until she learns to trust her gut and take chances on what makes her happy. This sugary-sweet movie might be new territory for Ziegler, but it’s exactly the type of film we’ve come to expect from Netflix. The streamer’s Christmas originals usually revolve around romance and family, with an aesthetic quality and winking irony that feels similar to Hallmark – the American card-maker turned movie giant, whose very name is synonymous with cliches.

articles.title: Rare panto programmes owned by 'Freddie Mercury of his time' sell at auction
articles.summary: The life of Henry Paget was the focus of the biopic Madfabulous released earlier this year.
body: A rare pair of pantomime programmes from the private theatre of a man dubbed "the Freddie Mercury of his time" have sold at auction for £3,600.
The 4th Marquess of Anglesey Henry Cyril Paget, also known as the Dancing Marquess, used his family home Plas Newydd, on Anglesey, to stage lavish productions free for local people.
His life was recently turned into a biopic, with Callum Scott Howells playing the aristocrat.
The programmes were for a production of Red Riding Hood and in the shapes of Little Red Riding Hood and Little Boy Blue.
